title: George Russell details fresh F1 target as title hopes dashed
excerpt:
George Russell has outlined his target of ending the F1 season with a streak of consistency as he sits on the verge of title defeat.

Russell entered the season as the favourite to walk away from the campaign with a maiden title in hand due to his experience over Kimi Antonelli and the lacklustre debut campaign the latter endured in 2025.

However, Antonelli has risen to the challenge and now needs just a ninth place on Sunday in Mexico to become the youngest champion in the sport's history.

Russell has had a mixed run of form of late. Having shown great speed to win in Baku, he has scored just six points in the three rounds since.

As he looks to a stronger 2027 campaign, Russell stated ending the current season on a high is his priority.

“It's definitely important for me to try and gain some consistency,” Russell told media including RacingNews365.

“A couple of races ago, we were on pole by eight tenths and won the race. Then, last week, I finished in P8.

“I've never had a season like this in my career where the performance has fluctuated so much.

“I know it's in there because you can't deliver performances like that in Baku if you've so-called lost it.

“It's just that we're struggling to have a high hit rate.

“We don't know why that is, and as I said, we've never had it. I've never had it personally before in my career. I guess that's probably the priority for me in these last few races.”

[Article continues below]

Russell points to Ferrari 'advantage' in Mexico

With his title hopes hanging by a thread and largely out of his control, Russell can do little but turn up at the track and fight as hard as he can.

Mexico City hosts round 19 of the campaign this weekend, with the city being a unique setting for F1 due to its high altitude.

Previewing the weekend, Russell predicted: “I think it's going to be very interesting.

“I think turbo lag is going to be a big factor for a lot of teams this weekend. There's obviously no secret that the likes of Ferrari have a smaller turbo than most, so they probably have quite an advantage in this regard.

“We're not sure as yet how challenging it will be, but I can definitely foresee it being not straightforward.”

title: Lewis Hamilton firmly rejects Mexico F1 theory surrounding Ferrari trick
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has firmly rejected the idea that Ferrari's smaller turbo is yielding stronger results in the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Coming into the weekend, it was expected that the 2026-spec power units would be given their greatest test thus far, owing to Mexico City being 2,285m above sea level - where air density is 25% lower than at sea level.

This means the engines, and specifically the turbochargers, must work harder to force air into the engine, with the phenomenon of turbo lag expected to be prevalent - this being the delay between power demand and the turbo spooling up enough to provide the requested power.

For 2026, this is set to be a harder challenge for the turbo as the MGU-H, which helped in eliminating turbo lag, has been removed from the power units.

For the Ferrari-powered cars on the grid, this was expected to be an advantage, with the turbo on the Ferrari unit smaller than that of rival engines, meaning the lag is, in theory, shortened.

However, following a Friday where team-mate Charles Leclerc topped both sessions, and Hamilton was fourth in FP1 before an engine gremlin struck in FP2, Hamilton rejected the idea.

"I don't really agree on the turbo thing," Hamilton explained.

"If you look at the speeds of the Mercedes and the Red Bull, they're still massive. They're still quicker at the end of the straights. Like they are at every race. So the turbo is just not making a difference.

"It's still pulling more at the end of the straights, so I think we're still losing a good couple of tenths, two or three tenths, but the car is behaving really well fundamentally. Our car is working well at tracks like this.

"I think the car feels like it's capable of competing in qualifying. But again, as I said, I don't know what it is they are able to do in qualifying. Everyone seems to take a step. I don't know if we can eke out a little bit more performance."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton on Ferrari engine issue

Turning to his stoppage mid-way through FP2, Hamilton explained that he was in the dark about the cause of the issue - but that his machine was feeling strong in his hands.

"They told me to stop. They saw some sort of problem, but it felt really good up until then," he said.

"The car was feeling great. I think we did a good job, made good setup changes, and the car was in a good place.

"My middle sector was strong, but even on my lap, we were losing power in a few places.

"I think I lost three-tenths. But [the bottom line] is that we've got a good car this weekend, so it is a shame to have lost this session."

title: Isack Hadjar summoned by F1 stewards over alleged paddock misconduct

title: Red Bull issue withering 'on fire' response to brutal Christian Horner comments
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has hit back at Christian Horner's claim that Red Bull has "lost its mojo" since the Briton's exit, insisting the team's spirit has never been stronger.

Horner, sacked as team principal and CEO in July last year and replaced by Mekies, has used recent media appearances to suggest the Milton Keynes squad had also lost "its presence and its vibe" since his departure.

Horner has described the atmosphere in his final period at Red Bull as unhappy and volatile, while also claiming executives had told him his operation had come to be seen as Christian Horner Racing rather than Red Bull Racing.

Mekies, who inherited a team battling chassis and power unit deficits, chronic start problems and radio issues through the first half of 2026, was asked to respond to Horner's comments and gave a pointed reply.

"First, Christian is entitled to his opinion," Mekies said, speaking to media, including RacingNews365.

"He obviously spent a lot of time with this team, and I respect his point of view.

"We certainly feel extremely differently about the vibe in the team. One of the strong points we have been enjoying, certainly in the last few months, is the incredible team spirit which has allowed us to come back from a very difficult moment."

[Article continues below]

Red Bull working off 'brutally honest comments' of drivers - Mekies

The Frenchman pointed to Red Bull's late-season turnaround last year, which saw Max Verstappen miss out on a fifth drivers' title by two points, and its resurgence this year after a sluggish start under the new regulations, as evidence of the spirit that exists.

"It's always one thing to have a positive spirit when you are winning races," said Mekies. "It's something else to have that same fighting spirit and unity between the team members when you are put under pressure, and we certainly had a challenging first part of the year, chassis side and PU side.

"The way the team stuck together, the way the team set the Milton Keynes departments on fire to try to come back, and the way they have done that in such a constructively challenging manner, from any of our team members to the brutally honest comments of our drivers, that's the Red Bull spirit, and that's certainly how we feel."

Mekies made clear, however, that the recent run of results, including wins for Verstappen in Singapore and Malaysia, is not being treated as mission accomplished.

"We need to go racing, and the guys have got the reward they deserved with the turnaround that they have produced, which is, I think, very remarkable," he said.

"Ultimately we are well aware that we live and die with our results, and the target is not to win one race or two races. The target is to be back to winning world titles, and until we are there, nobody will feel we have achieved anything."

title: Ferrari call for track changes at 'almost dangerous' Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur called for track changes to be made overnight at the Mexico City Grand Prix, arguing that some of the bumps are "almost dangerous" at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Despite an afternoon of mixed fortunes for the Scuderia, with Charles Leclerc topping both FP1 and FP2 and Lewis Hamilton's SF-26 grinding to a halt in the second hour of running, Vasseur was more concerned with the condition of the circuit.

He highlighted how some of the bumps proved treacherous, and advocated remedial work before FP3, which is not uncommon in F1.

Issues with track surfaces do crop up, and venues are usually receptive to making changes and quick to implement them.

Reflecting on the opening two sessions of the weekend, Vasseur was keen to downplay the pace seen from Leclerc, dismissing the idea that the Italian team should carry any confidence into the second day of running.

"I don't have to be confident or not. We have to work. We have to try to get the best for [FP3 and qualifying]," Vasseur said after FP2. "Conditions are mega extreme. That we knew before with the altitude; it's a challenge.

"It's a challenge for us, but also for the others. It means that we have a lot of work to do... and it's mega bumpy."

Expanding on that last remark, the Ferrari boss pinpointed the most concerning part of the track, where he would most like to see action taken before FP3, after numerous cars were seen bottoming out over the bump heading into the first corner.

"Probably a bit too much before Turn 1," the Frenchman added. "It's almost dangerous. We will have to do something [before FP3].

"But overall, I think that it was a good start to the weekend, but still a long way to go."

title: Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson hit with double penalties for 'unacceptable' Mexico clash
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have both been hit with a one-place grid penalty for the Mexico City Grand Prix, and handed a penalty point apiece, following their needless clash in second practice.

Just 13 minutes into FP2, and on approach to the stadium complex at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Verstappen opted to dive down the inside at Turn 12 on a driver who was his Red Bull team-mate for three races only recently, due to Isack Hadjar sustaining a wrist injury.

Lawson, though, held his ground in his Racing Bulls machinery and jostled with Verstappen through the slow Turn 13 before the Red Bull driver ran over the right edge of the Racing Bulls' front wing at Turn 14, depositing debris on the circuit which needed to be cleared by marshals.

Verstappen claimed that Lawson's move "wasn't smart" when addressing the media before heading to the stewards to account for his actions.

Ultimately, the stewards decided that the move was considered "unacceptable" following a warning given to the team managers earlier in the day - with both drivers being handed a one-place grid drop and one penalty point on their super licences.

"The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 3 (Max Verstappen), the driver of Car 30 (Liam Lawson), team representatives and reviewed video evidence," began the verdict.

"On the approach to turn 12 car 3 was on a preparation lap and car 30 was on a cool down lap preparing for another push lap. The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the Stewards, particularly in view of the warning that had been given at the Team Managers meeting earlier this day.

"Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and “clumsy”.

"Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the Stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty, particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years.

"Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits."
